source_refs.note: Book p. 190-191: 6.4.1 Key Features of the Ellipse (foci, centre, vertices, co-vertices, symmetry, eccentricity, directrices, latus rectum, parametric form, foci on y-axis), relation of a, b, e, circle, second definition, Figure 6.16, Note

items: Foci: The foci are at \((\pm c, 0)\), where \(c^2 = a^2 - b^2\).
Centre: The midpoint \(C\) of the segment joining the foci is called the centre. For the equation above, the centre is at the origin \((0, 0)\).
Vertices: Setting \(y = 0\) gives \(x = \pm a\). The points \(A'(-a, 0)\) and \(A(a, 0)\) are the vertices. The line segment \(A'A\) of length \(2a\) is the major axis.

Co-vertices: Setting \(x = 0\) gives \(y = \pm b\). The points \(B'(0, -b)\) and \(B(0, b)\) are called the co-vertices. The line segment \(B'B\) of length \(2b\) is the minor axis. Since \(a > b\), the major axis is longer than the minor axis.
Symmetry: The equation is unchanged if \(x\) is replaced by \(-x\) and \(y\) by \(-y\); hence the ellipse is symmetric about the x-axis, y-axis, and the origin.
Eccentricity: The eccentricity \(e\) of an ellipse is defined as \(e = \frac{c}{a}\). Since \(a > c > 0\), we have \(0 < e < 1\).
Directrices: For the ellipse \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\) with \(a > b\), there are two directrices given by the vertical lines \(x = \pm\frac{a}{e}\).
Latus Rectum: Each of the focal chords perpendicular to the major axis is called a latus rectum (plural: latera recta). The length of each latus rectum is \(\frac{2b^2}{a}\).

Parametric Equations: For all real \(\theta\), the point \((a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)\) lies on the ellipse \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\). Thus, the parametric equations of the ellipse are: \(x = a\cos\theta,\ y = b\sin\theta\).

Foci on the y-axis: If the foci are on the y-axis at \((0, \pm c)\), the roles of \(a\) and \(b\) are interchanged, and the standard equation becomes \(\frac{x^2}{b^2} + \frac{y^2}{a^2} = 1\), \(a > b\): with vertices \((0, \pm a)\), and covertices \((\pm b, 0)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read these features: \(a\) is the distance from the centre to a vertex (along the long axis), \(b\) is the distance from the centre to a co-vertex (along the short axis), and \(c\) is the distance from the centre to a focus. The foci always lie on the major axis, inside the ellipse, because \(c < a\).
Why is the ellipse symmetric? Only \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) appear in the equation, and \((-x)^2 = x^2\), \((-y)^2 = y^2\). So if \((x, y)\) is on the curve, so are \((-x, y)\), \((x, -y)\) and \((-x, -y)\).
Eccentricity measures how flat the ellipse is. If \(e\) is close to 0, \(c\) is tiny, the foci are near the centre and the ellipse is almost a circle. If \(e\) is close to 1, \(c\) is almost \(a\) and the ellipse is long and thin.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where does \(\frac{2b^2}{a}\) come from? The latus rectum through \(F(c, 0)\) is the vertical line \(x = c\). Put \(x = c\) in the equation:
\[\frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 - \frac{c^2}{a^2} = \frac{a^2 - c^2}{a^2} = \frac{b^2}{a^2}\]
so \(y = \pm\frac{b^2}{a}\). The chord goes from \((c, -\frac{b^2}{a})\) to \((c, \frac{b^2}{a})\), so its length is \(\frac{2b^2}{a}\).
Why does \((a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)\) lie on the ellipse? Substitute: \(\frac{a^2\cos^2\theta}{a^2} + \frac{b^2\sin^2\theta}{b^2} = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\).
The directrices \(x = \pm\frac{a}{e}\) lie outside the ellipse, because \(e < 1\) makes \(\frac{a}{e} > a\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
Horizontal or vertical? Look at the denominators. The larger denominator is always \(a^2\). If it is under \(x^2\), the major axis is along the x-axis; if it is under \(y^2\), the major axis is along the y-axis.
Example: in \(\frac{x^2}{16} + \frac{y^2}{25} = 1\) the larger number 25 is under \(y^2\), so \(a = 5\), \(b = 4\), the foci are \((0, \pm 3)\) and the vertices \((0, \pm 5)\).
Relation between a, b and e: Since \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2\), setting \(c = ae \Rightarrow b^2 = a^2 - a^2e^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)\).
bold: Relation between a, b and e:

blocks.text: Circle as a Special Case: If the foci coincide, then \(c = 0\) and \(a = b\), so the ellipse becomes a circle with radius \(r = a = b\), and has equation: \(x^2 + y^2 = a^2\). Clearly for circle \(e = 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The relation \(b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)\) is useful when \(a\) and \(e\) are given: you get \(b\) without first finding \(c\). For a circle the two foci join at the centre, so \(c = 0\) and \(e = \frac{0}{a} = 0\): a circle is the roundest possible ellipse.

Second definition of ellipse: The ellipse can also be defined as, if a point \(P\) moves such that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point \(F\) (the focus) to its distance from a fixed straight line (the directrix) is equal to a constant, \(e\) (less than 1), the locus of \(P\) is an ellipse of eccentricity \(e\).
That is, if \(\frac{|PF|}{|PM|} = e\), where \(0 < e < 1\), the locus of \(P\) is an ellipse.

blocks.alt: An ellipse with focus F inside it and a vertical directrix line outside it on the right. A point P on the ellipse is joined to F (segment marked e) and to the foot M of the perpendicular on the directrix (segment marked 1), with a right angle at M.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The equation of ellipse can also be derived using the above definition.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This is the focus-directrix definition, the same idea as for the parabola. The only difference is the ratio: for a parabola \(|PF| = |PM|\) (ratio 1), for an ellipse \(|PF|\) is a fixed fraction \(e < 1\) of \(|PM|\).
Check it at the vertex \(A(a, 0)\) with focus \(F(ae, 0)\) and directrix \(x = \frac{a}{e}\): \(|AF| = a - ae = a(1 - e)\) and \(|AM| = \frac{a}{e} - a = \frac{a(1 - e)}{e}\). So \(\frac{|AF|}{|AM|} = e\), exactly as the definition says.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
For \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\), \(a > b\): vertices \((\pm a, 0)\), co-vertices \((0, \pm b)\), foci \((\pm c, 0)\) with \(c^2 = a^2 - b^2\).
Major axis \(2a\), minor axis \(2b\), eccentricity \(e = \frac{c}{a}\) with \(0 < e < 1\), \(b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)\).
Directrices \(x = \pm\frac{a}{e}\) (outside the ellipse), latus rectum length \(\frac{2b^2}{a}\), parametric point \((a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)\).
If the larger denominator is under \(y^2\), every \(x\)-feature becomes the matching \(y\)-feature.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Taking \(a\) from the denominator under \(x^2\) every time. \(a^2\) is the larger denominator, wherever it stands.
Writing the directrices as \(x = \pm ae\). That is the focus; the directrix is \(x = \pm\frac{a}{e}\).
Writing the latus rectum length as \(\frac{2a^2}{b}\); it is \(\frac{2b^2}{a}\) (the shorter one).
